title: Not everyone agreed: Albo's three roots
hookLine: Crescas and Albo proposed other lists; the streams read the principles differently
carry: crescas and albo argued from inside, and stayed

cards: Three. Not thirteen. A Spanish rabbi named Joseph Albo read Maimonides' list carefully, with respect, and then wrote a whole book arguing that Judaism rests on three roots.

Tradition says Albo studied with another sharp reader, Hasdai Crescas, who questioned the list from a different angle. Neither one walked away from Judaism. They stayed inside it and argued about its foundations.
Today's lesson is in the title, and it's a habit this tradition keeps.

teach.b: Not everyone agreed. Start with Crescas. In his book, The Light of the LORD, he asked a hard question about the very first principle.
The Torah gives commandments. But can you command someone to believe God exists? A command already assumes someone is commanding.

So for Crescas, God's existence is the ground the commandments stand on, not one more item among them. He sorted beliefs differently, into roots, foundations and true beliefs, not one flat list. Next, Albo.
His book is called Sefer HaIkkarim, the Book of Roots.

He kept many of Maimonides' ideas but counted only three roots: God exists, the Torah is from heaven, and there is reward and punishment. The others, he said, grow out of these, like branches from a trunk.

teach.h: THE STREAMS READ THE LIST DIFFERENTLY.
teach.b: Then, the streams today. Some Jews hold the thirteen as written, and say them as written. Some read certain lines, such as the dead living again or the Torah from heaven, in other ways.
Some put practice and community at the center and hold belief more loosely. Each says why, from its own reading of the tradition. And notice one more thing.

teach.h: THE LIST STAYS ON THE TABLE.
teach.b: The arguers didn't throw the list away. They kept it on the table, so they could keep arguing with it. Agreeing on which questions matter can hold a people together, even when the answers differ.

how: Jewish students read Maimonides' principles alongside the works of his critics, such as Crescas's Or Adonai and Albo's Sefer HaIkkarim; the different movements of Judaism explain in their own writings how they understand the principles.

games.q: you're Joseph Albo. you respect Maimonides, but you think thirteen principles is too many. what do you do?
o: say nothing and follow the list.
write a book proposing three roots, with the rest growing out of them.
games.why: he writes the Book of Roots: three roots, with the other beliefs growing from them like branches.

practice: Ask yourself quietly what you stand on: not what you're supposed to say, but what actually holds you up on a hard day.
It might be a belief, a person, a promise, a practice; there's no right number, since Maimonides counted thirteen and Albo three. Rest on what you find.
